# i18n translation backlog

This document is generated, not maintained: `go generate ./internal/i18n` rewrites it from the
tables, and `go run ./cmd/qki18n -check` — which TestBacklogDocumentIsCurrent runs as part of the
ordinary `go test ./...` — fails when the committed file no longer matches them. Nothing in it is
hand-copied, so a row that gets filled in disappears from here by itself.

It lists the untranslated backlog the migration froze rather than fixed, most valuable first. The
three counts are the three ratchets, measured over the same tables: when a row stops being listed,
the ratchet that counted it can be lowered — to the value a run measures, never to a value somebody
hopes for.

| Section | Rows | Ratchet | Limit today |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Placeholders in a different order than the English (live defects) | 11 | `TestVerbSequenceMatches` | 11 |
| 2. Imported rows whose Chinese repeats the English | 25 | `TestProofUntranslatedImportsAreCounted` | 25 |
| 3. Field-message rows whose Chinese repeats the English | 64 | `TestProofUntranslatedFieldMessagesAreCounted` | 64 |
| **total** | **100** | | |

Read them in order. The first is a defect being shipped right now; the other two are work that has
to come from a speaker of Chinese. Each row names the table and the column to edit, and section 1
states which placeholder has to change position — a specification, not a translation.

  fix — the moved word order has to read correctly in the sentence that is left — and the consequence
  of getting it wrong is not cosmetic: a reader under `QK_LANG=zh` sees the wrong words in the wrong
  slots.

## 2. Imported rows whose Chinese repeats the English

For these 25 rows the `zh` column repeats the `en` column. That is not a translation and not a
defect of the migration: the message shipped English-only before it had an id, so inventing Chinese
would have changed what a reader sees. The value has to come from a speaker.

The last column is measured, not assumed. The generator scans every `.go`, `.tsv` and `.md` file in
this repository and in the pinned syntax layer, keeps the ones that contain Han characters, and asks
whether a Chinese rendering of *this* message exists. A rendering is looked up by the message's own
text with its format verbs collapsed to one wildcard, because a rendering written down elsewhere may
say `%s` where this row says `%q`; such a find is reported as a near match, with the hash of its
canonical form so the copy can be identified without printing Chinese into a Go source file. Being
one id away is not being the same message: `StringIndexOutOfBoundsError` is not
`IndexOutOfBoundsError`, and a row that merely looks like a neighbour is reported as what the scan
found, not as a translation that exists.

## 3. Field-message rows whose Chinese repeats the English

For these 64 rows the `zh` column repeats the `en` column. That is not a translation and not a
defect of the migration: the message shipped English-only before it had an id, so inventing Chinese
would have changed what a reader sees. The value has to come from a speaker.

The last column is measured, not assumed. The generator scans every `.go`, `.tsv` and `.md` file in
this repository and in the pinned syntax layer, keeps the ones that contain Han characters, and asks
whether a Chinese rendering of *this* message exists. A rendering is looked up by the message's own
text with its format verbs collapsed to one wildcard, because a rendering written down elsewhere may
say `%s` where this row says `%q`; such a find is reported as a near match, with the hash of its
canonical form so the copy can be identified without printing Chinese into a Go source file. Being
one id away is not being the same message: `StringIndexOutOfBoundsError` is not
`IndexOutOfBoundsError`, and a row that merely looks like a neighbour is reported as what the scan
found, not as a translation that exists.

## How to fill this in

1. **Edit the `zh` column of the row's table.** Each row names its table in its *Row to edit* line;
   the columns are tab-separated and `zh` is the last column on the row. For a `local` row the `src`
   column must keep repeating the `en` column, so only `zh` changes. Never edit
   `internal/i18n/msg_gen.go`: it is generated, and the next `go generate` discards the edit.
2. **Re-run the generator.** `go generate ./internal/i18n` rewrites both the catalog and this document.
   `go run ./cmd/qki18n -check` then fails while either of them is stale — that gate is what keeps
   this list honest. `go test ./... -count=1` runs the same check through TestGeneratedCatalogIsCurrent
   and TestBacklogDocumentIsCurrent.
3. **Lower a ratchet limit only to a number a run measured.** Each section's ratchet is the test named
   in the summary table above, in `internal/i18n/`; its `allowed` constant may only shrink, and the
   test prints the count it measured. Setting the limit to the number of rows still listed here, or to
   a round number, is how a ratchet stops guarding anything.
4. **A row in section 1 needs the sentence re-authored, not the placeholders swapped.** The Chinese
   moves a verb or a type out of position, so the words around the placeholders have to move with
   them; the *Placeholder position report* says which position must hold which placeholder, and that
   is the whole specification. Getting the order wrong is not a cosmetic defect: the call site binds
   its arguments by position, so under `QK_LANG=zh` the reader sees the wrong words in the wrong
   slots — for example the row whose id ends in `using_q_on_s_not_supported` under the compiler
   domain prints the operator where the type belongs.
5. **Every user-facing message goes through an id path.** Wiring a message that is still a literal at
   its call site is a separate change: `internal/i18n/fieldpass_test.go` fails on a message literal
   written into a struct field, and `TestDecouplingRatchet` fails on a text-keyed entry point coming
   back.

## How this document is kept true

`cmd/qki18n` renders the catalog and this document from the same tables in one run, and `-check`
compares both against what is committed. The call sites and the "found elsewhere" column are measured
by scanning the checkout at generation time, so they move when the code moves: a message whose call
site disappears is reported as `unknown` rather than silently keeping a stale line number, and a
translation added anywhere in either tree shows up as a hit on the row it translates.

Two limits are worth knowing. A rendering that is assembled at run time (`fmt.Sprintf` of a prefix and
a suffix) is not a single line and will not be found; and the scan reads `.go`, `.tsv` and `.md` files,
so a rendering that lives only in a generated artefact or a history revision is out of its reach.
Neither case is reported as a translation.
